brave-llmcontext.snippet:
The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set ($\bot$) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths.
Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion. This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches.
We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations.

# Title:Sound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers
This paper formally specifies the tnum abstract domain and its arithmetic operators. We provide the first proofs of soundness and optimality of the abstract arithmetic operators for tnum addition and subtraction used in the BPF analyzer. Further, we describe a novel sound algorithm for multiplication of tnums that is more precise and efficient (runs 33% faster on average) than the Linux kernel's algorithm.

# numeric-domains: abstract domains for fixed-width numeric values
- Tnum: known-value/unknown-mask tracking numbers. Arithmetic wraps at 64 bits and shift counts are reduced modulo 64.
- Znum: tracks whether each bit may be zero and/or one. Arithmetic wraps at 64 bits and shift counts are reduced modulo 64.
- Rnum: a range representation with independent signed and unsigned bounds.
- WrappedInterval: one interval on the circle of integers modulo 2^64.
- RangeSet<K>: a bounded union of disjoint intervals; its capacity is a direct storage/precision tradeoff.
- BitRange<K>: an experimental reduced product of RangeSet and Tnum.
All three domains provide constant and membership queries, extrema, and signed/unsigned bound inspection. They also provide union (the least representable domain containing both operands) and intersection (the values common to both operands), including empty intersections. Tnum and Znum additionally supports bitwise operations and basic unsigned arithmetic.

 Developing a Self-Report Outcome Measure for Complementary and Alternative Medicine  

 Objective: Our objective was to develop a pilot measure of subjective outcomes of complementary and alternative medicine (CAM). Current options for assessing subjective outcomes in CAM are either too burdensome or fail to represent diverse outcomes. A single measure specifying common, patient-reported outcomes of CAM would be of value. Design: We conducted a three-phase instrument development study. In phase I, 30 CAM-receiving patients and 12 CAM practitioners completed a battery of standardized measures. Participants identified those standardized items relevant to CAM outcome and suggested additional outcome issues. In phase II, 20 CAM-receiving patients completed a Q-sort to determine which items from phase I were most relevant to CAM outcome. In phase III, five experts reviewed the items from phase II for content validity. Setting: An integrative medicine clinic at a private, Midwest US hospital. Participants: CAM patients, practitioners, and researchers and an outcomes measurement specialist. Results: In phase I, 30 standardized items were judged relevant to CAM outcome, and 8 additional items were suggested. In phase II, 29 of the 38 phase I items were deemed at least \"moderately relevant\" to CAM outcome. In phase III, experts added 15 items, dropped 9 items, and altered 3 items. The 35 resulting items were classified into content domains, forming a testable, pilot version of the instrument.

ceramic.snippet: The content (regular text) is what's important to the reader, but it needs to be presented in a meaningful way. XML helps the computer format the document to make it more comprehensible to humans. page 7 Learning XML 1.1.2 Documents When you hear the word document, you probably think of a sequence of words partitioned into paragraphs, sections, and chapters, comprising a human-readable record such as a book, article, or essay. But in XML, a document is even more general: it's the basic unit of XML information, composed of elements and other markup in an orderly package. It can contain text such as a story or article, but it doesn't have to. Instead, it might consist of a database of numbers, or some abstract structure representing a molecule or equation. In fact, one of the most promising applications of XML is as a format for application-to-application data exchange. We conducted five focus groups of six to eight participants each, with users of CAM recruited through experienced CAM providers and clinics. Eligible participants were aged 21 or older, had used CAM in the last 12 months, and believed the treatment to be beneficial. In addition, participants identified empowerment, increased hope and spiritual growth as results of receiving CAM treatments. A new behavioral health outcome domain emerged as participants reported that CAM use had fostered behavioral changes such as increased exercise, smoking cessation and improving their diets. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set (⊥) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion. This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier’s abstract domains to prune dead branches. keenable.title: Sound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers
keenable.snippet: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) is a language and run-time system that allows non-superusers to extend the Linux and Windows operating systems by downloading user code into the kernel. To ensure that user code is safe to run in kernel context, BPF relies on a static analyzer that proves properties about the code, such as bounded memory access and the absence of operations that crash. The BPF static analyzer checks safety using abstract interpretation with several abstract domains. Among these, the domain of tnums (tristate numbers) is a key domain used to reason about the bitwise uncertainty in program values. This paper formally specifies the tnum abstract domain and its arithmetic operators. We provide the first proofs of soundness and optimality of the abstract arithmetic operators for tnum addition and subtraction used in the BPF analyzer. Further, we describe a novel sound algorithm for multiplication of tnums that is more precise and efficient (runs 33% faster on average) than the Linux kernel's algorithm. Our tnum multiplication is now merged in the Linux kernel.

keenable.title: A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
keenable.snippet: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.

keenable.title: Constrained Abstract Domain for Neural Network Verification
keenable.snippet:
Neural network verification (NNV) formally verifies that a network satisfies a specified property for all inputs within a defined region. Modern NNV tools employ *abstract domains* to compute a sound over-approximation of the network’s behavior from the given input region, thus the tightness of these abstractions essentially determines efficiency. A long line of increasingly precise domains has been developed, but they all describe the valid input region in the same restrictive way, *e.g.*, an ℓ_p-norm ball. A practical input region is rarely a simple ℓ_p ball, but rather a combination ℓ_p ball with additional constraints. Verifying a network over such a region with existing abstraction produces a loose over-approximation, which results in either failing to verify a property or spurious counterexamples. We introduce *Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain* (Clad), a new abstract domain that computes a sound over-approximation of neural networks over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. Clad propagates these constraints and tightens bounds over the true feasible region. However, bounding a neuron over the intersection of these constraints has no closed-form solution, so Clad relaxes each constraint into the objective with a Lagrange multiplier and solves the resulting max-min problem with a projected primal-dual method, alternating a projected gradient step on the input with a multiplier update.

In this work, we propose *Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain* (Clad), a new abstract domain that verifies DNNs over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. Clad propagates these constraints through the network and tightens every neuron’s bounds over the true feasible region, *e.g.*, the combination of all the input constraints.

keenable-realtime.snippet: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) is a language and run-time system that allows non-superusers to extend the Linux and Windows operating systems by downloading user code into the kernel. To ensure that user code is safe to run in kernel context, BPF relies on a static analyzer that proves properties about the code, such as bounded memory access and the absence of operations that crash. The BPF static analyzer checks safety using abstract interpretation with several abstract domains. Among these, the domain of tnums (tristate numbers) is a key domain used to reason about the bitwise uncertainty in program values. This paper formally specifies the tnum abstract domain and its arithmetic operators. We provide the first proofs of soundness and optimality of the abstract arithmetic operators for tnum addition and subtraction used in the BPF analyzer. Further, we describe a novel sound algorithm for multiplication of tnums that is more precise and efficient (runs 33% faster on average) than the Linux kernel's algorithm. Our tnum multiplication is now merged in the Linux kernel.

keenable-realtime.title: A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
keenable-realtime.snippet: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.

keenable-realtime.snippet:
Neural network verification (NNV) formally verifies that a network satisfies a specified property for all inputs within a defined region. Modern NNV tools employ *abstract domains* to compute a sound over-approximation of the network’s behavior from the given input region, thus the tightness of these abstractions essentially determines efficiency. A long line of increasingly precise domains has been developed, but they all describe the valid input region in the same restrictive way, *e.g.*, an ℓ_p-norm ball. A practical input region is rarely a simple ℓ_p ball, but rather a combination ℓ_p ball with additional constraints. Verifying a network over such a region with existing abstraction produces a loose over-approximation, which results in either failing to verify a property or spurious counterexamples. We introduce *Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain* (Clad), a new abstract domain that computes a sound over-approximation of neural networks over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. Clad propagates these constraints and tightens bounds over the true feasible region. However, bounding a neuron over the intersection of these constraints has no closed-form solution, so Clad relaxes each constraint into the objective with a Lagrange multiplier and solves the resulting max-min problem with a projected primal-dual method, alternating a projected gradient step on the input with a multiplier update.

Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
Abstract
Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. Abstract
Distinct proofs, programs, formulas, or rewrite paths may have the same observable behavior while differing in their occurrence structure, sharing, interfaces, or transformation history. Reduced product of abstract domains is a rather well-known operation for domain composition in abstract interpretation. The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set ($\bot$) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion. This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches. We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.

Written by Eric Normand. Published: April 28, 2022.

## Reflections 🤔

*You need two abstractions to model*

When you model a domain in your software, you create two abstractions. Let's see an example. We'll use the domain of days of the week, as we saw last time. We'll model them as the numbers 0-6.

The first abstraction is mapping the days of the week to the numbers.


```
Concrete domain => Abstract domain
----------------------------------
Monday     => 0
Tuesday    => 1
Wednesday   => 2
Thursday    => 3
Friday     => 4
Saturday    => 5
Sunday     => 6

```

Abstraction is a mapping from one representation to another, known as the concrete and abstract domains. This one maps the days of the week (already an abstract concept, but we call that the concrete domain since it's what we're mapping *from*) to the numbers 0-6 (numbers are also an abstract concept, and we call it the abstract domain since it's what we're mapping *to*).

That's the first abstraction. The second abstraction goes from bits in our computer to numbers.


```
Concrete domain => Abstract domain
----------------------------------
0000      => 0
0001      => 1
0010      => 2
0011      => 3
0100      => 4
0101      => 5
0110      => 6

```

There's an interpretation of bits as binary representations of numbers. Luckily, our machines come with that built-in, and our languages have arithmetic operations to take advantage of them. In essence, we get this particular mapping for free. It lets us pretend we're dealing with the abstract domain when manipulating bits. And we can live the fiction until our numbers get too big (integer overflow).

Here are our two mappings:


```
Days of the week => Integers 0-6
Bits             => Integers 0-6

```

Because our two mappings share an abstract domain, we know we can represent days of the week in bits.

## Fundamentals of Abstract Interpretation

Abstract interpretation is a theory underpinning static analysis that approximates program semantics via abstract models. It enables reasoning about program properties without execution, crucial for verifying software correctness in safety-critical or resource-constrained environments.

## 1. Foundations of Abstract Interpretation

Abstract interpretation formalizes program analysis by mapping concrete program states to an abstract domain. The abstraction must balance precision and computational cost, as overly precise domains can be intractable, while coarse abstractions may yield useless results.

### 1.1 Abstract Domains

Abstract domains represent program state properties with mathematical structures. The choice affects analysis scalability and precision. Common domains include:

- **Intervals:** Efficient for numeric ranges but limited in relational expressiveness.
- **Polyhedra:** Capture linear constraints but suffer from high computational overhead.
- **Finite Sets:** Model discrete states but can explode combinatorially.

Misuse often occurs when selecting domains without considering the program's characteristics, leading to either excessive false positives or impractical analysis times.

### 1.2 Galois Connections

Galois connections formalize the abstraction-concretization relationship via monotonic functions:

- `α: C → A` (abstraction function)
- `γ: A → C` (concretization function)

They ensure soundness by guaranteeing that abstract elements safely over-approximate concrete semantics. However, establishing these functions can be non-trivial for complex domains.

seltz.snippet:
In computer science, **abstract interpretation** is a theory of sound approximation of the semantics of computer programs, based on monotonic functions over ordered sets, especially lattices. It can be viewed as a partial execution of a computer program which gains information about its semantics (e.g., control-flow, data-flow) without performing all the calculations.

Its main concrete application is formal static analysis, the automatic extraction of information about the possible executions of computer programs; such analyses have two main usages:

- inside compilers, to analyse programs to decide whether certain optimizations or transformations are applicable;
- for debugging or even the certification of programs against classes of bugs.

Abstract interpretation was formalized by the French computer scientists Patrick Cousot and Radhia Cousot in the late 1970s.

## Intuition

This section illustrates abstract interpretation by means of real-world, non-computing examples.

Consider the people in a conference room. Assume a unique identifier for each person in the room, like a social security number in the United States. ## Introduction to Abstract Interpretation

Abstract Interpretation approximates program behaviors by mapping concrete program states to abstract domains, enabling static analysis without enumerating all executions. This abstraction trades precision for tractability, often leading to conservative over-approximations.

## Basic Concepts

- **Abstract Domains:** Mathematical structures representing simplified program state properties, such as intervals or sign abstractions.
- **Galois Connections:** Formal relationships linking concrete and abstract domains, ensuring soundness of the abstraction.

## Abstract Domains

Abstract domains represent sets of possible values compactly. For example, instead of tracking exact integer values of a variable `x`, an interval domain might represent `x` as `[0, +∞)` to indicate non-negativity.

```
let x = 5;
```

Abstract interpretation would represent `x` as:

```
{ x | x ≥ 0 }
```

Note that abstract domains must balance expressiveness and computational cost. For instance, interval domains are efficient but cannot represent disjoint value sets, which can lead to imprecise results.

## Galois Connections

A Galois connection consists of two monotone functions:

- `α: Concrete Domain → Abstract Domain` (abstraction)
- `γ: Abstract Domain → Concrete Domain` (concretization)

They satisfy:

α(c) ≤ a \iff c ≤ γ(a)

This ensures soundness: the abstract domain safely over-approximates the concrete semantics. However, completeness is rarely achievable in practice due to undecidability and complexity.

```
int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}
```

Using an interval domain, if `a ∈ [1, 3]` and `b ∈ [2, 4]`, then the output is abstracted as:

```
{ x | x ∈ [3, 7] }
```

This abstraction avoids enumerating all input pairs but may lose precision if domains are too coarse.

ultimate.title: Sound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers
ultimate.snippet: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) is a language and run-time system that allows non-superusers to extend the Linux and Windows operating systems by downloading user code into the kernel. To ensure that user code is safe to run in kernel context, BPF relies on a static analyzer that proves properties about the code, such as bounded memory access and the absence of operations that crash. The BPF static analyzer checks safety using abstract interpretation with several abstract domains. Among these, the domain of tnums (tristate numbers) is a key domain used to reason about the bitwise uncertainty in program values. This paper formally specifies the tnum abstract domain and its arithmetic operators. We provide the first proofs of soundness and optimality of the abstract arithmetic operators for tnum addition and subtraction used in the BPF analyzer. Further, we describe a novel sound algorithm for multiplication of tnums that is more precise and efficient (runs 33% faster on average) than the Linux kernel's algorithm. Our tnum multiplication is now merged in the Linux kernel.

ultimate.title: A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
ultimate.snippet: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.

ultimate.title: Constrained Abstract Domain for Neural Network Verification
ultimate.snippet:
Neural network verification (NNV) formally verifies that a network satisfies a specified property for all inputs within a defined region. Modern NNV tools employ *abstract domains* to compute a sound over-approximation of the network’s behavior from the given input region, thus the tightness of these abstractions essentially determines efficiency. A long line of increasingly precise domains has been developed, but they all describe the valid input region in the same restrictive way, *e.g.*, an ℓ_p-norm ball. A practical input region is rarely a simple ℓ_p ball, but rather a combination ℓ_p ball with additional constraints. Verifying a network over such a region with existing abstraction produces a loose over-approximation, which results in either failing to verify a property or spurious counterexamples. We introduce *Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain* (Clad), a new abstract domain that computes a sound over-approximation of neural networks over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. Clad propagates these constraints and tightens bounds over the true feasible region. However, bounding a neuron over the intersection of these constraints has no closed-form solution, so Clad relaxes each constraint into the objective with a Lagrange multiplier and solves the resulting max-min problem with a projected primal-dual method, alternating a projected gradient step on the input with a multiplier update.

In this work, we propose *Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain* (Clad), a new abstract domain that verifies DNNs over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. Clad propagates these constraints through the network and tightens every neuron’s bounds over the true feasible region, *e.g.*, the combination of all the input constraints.

ultimate.title: Abstract String Domain Defined with Word Equations as a Reduced Product
ultimate.snippet: We introduce a string-interval abstract domain, where string intervals are characterized by systems of word equations (encoding lower bounds on string values) and word disequalities (encoding upper bounds). Building upon the lattice structure of string intervals, we define an abstract string object as a reduced product on a string property semilattice, determined by length-non-increasing morphisms. We consider several reduction strategies for abstract string objects and show that upon these strategies the string object domain forms a lattice. We define basic abstract string operations on the domain, aiming to minimize computational overheads on the reduction, and show how the domain can be used to analyse properties of JavaScript string manipulating programs.

A constant-time emptiness check for the Linux eBPF verifier using abstract step functions to prune dead paths. 45/100Research signal⌘ Code released▲ Claims SOTA · Domain-specific formal verification improvement for Linux eBPF verifier.
We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask.
Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.

you.title: Sound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers
you.snippet:
To ensure that user code is safe to run in kernel context, BPF relies on a static analyzer that proves properties about the code, such as bounded memory access and the absence of operations that crash. The BPF static analyzer checks safety using abstract interpretation with several abstract domains. Among these, the domain of tnums (tristate numbers) is a key domain used to reason about the bitwise uncertainty in program values.
This paper formally specifies the tnum abstract domain and its arithmetic operators. We provide the first proofs of soundness and optimality of the abstract arithmetic operators for tnum addition and subtraction used in the BPF analyzer. Further, we describe a novel sound algorithm for multiplication of tnums that is more precise and efficient (runs 33% faster on average) than the Linux kernel’s algorithm.
Our tnum multiplication is now merged in the Linux kernel. Abstract domains, Program verification, Static analysis, Kernel extensions, eBPF
